newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy tells Albanians -- "No troublemakers please".
newsitem.headline: Italy tells Albanians -- "No troublemakers please".

text.p: Coastguards rescued more than 800 Albanians from a stricken ship on Monday as refugees from the country's unrest continued to flee across Adriatic to Italy.

The coastguards said 1,500 refugees arrived in the southern ports of Brindisi and Otranto on Monday alone, and more were on their way, pushing the total who have made the crossing to escape this month's armed chaos to more than 6,000.

The U.S. Navy said its forces in the Adriatic had also picked up 85 Albanians from two stricken boats on Sunday, including one which capsized with 55 men on board. Marine and Navy swimmers had to rescue them from the water.

Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi, eager to prevent a repeat of the mass influx of Albanians in 1991 after the collapse of communism, said his country wanted to make sure the latest arrivals did not include criminals.
"We want to take in those who really need it but not those...who cause problems," Prodi told Italian reporters in Damascus where he is on an official visit.
Italy already has a big problem with clandestine immigration from Albania, often involving drugs-running.
It has played a key role in Western efforts to end the unrest in the Balkan state and Prodi said he hoped conditions could soon return to normal so refugees could go home.
"We are firm in our decision not to open the door indiscriminately," he said.
His deputy, Walter Veltroni, on a visit to Brindisi, said Italy would deal "severely" with non-humanitarian cases.
Italy signalled a tougher stance when the captain and crew of a fishing boat with 142 Albanians aboard were arrested on Sunday for bringing in illegal immigrants and firearms.
"Today we're taking in people who are fleeing Albania because the conditions there...do not guarantee their safety," Veltroni said.
"As soon as...we manage to rebuild some conditions of security in Albania, it's clear our motivation will change."
Charity organisations struggling to care for refugees in makeshift reception centres said they were being overwhelmed and tourist officials said the influx was proving bad for business.
"The Albanian crisis is causing serious headaches for the tourist sector. Some foreign tour operators are cancelling bookings," said regional tourism official Rossana Di Bello.
A European Union-led diplomatic mission flew to Tirana from Brindisi on Monday for talks on how to help the new broad-based government end the anarchy in the Balkan state.

But the exodus continued and coastguards mounted their second major operation in as many days to rescue more than 800 Albanians crammed like sardines on a decrepit navy ship after it took on water. All were ferried ashore and the ship later sank.
The 40-metre (133-foot) vessel would normally hold up to 50 people. "It's absurd to put so many people on such a small, old and unseaworthy vessel," said coastguard captain Ugo D'Atri.

Coastguards in the northern Adriatic port of Ravenna said 24 refugees, including 11 children, had docked on Monday in a cargo ship from the troubled Albanian port of Durres. Several hundred refugees also arrived in the southern port of Otranto.
